samples.summary: API-key listing is only `assertMember`-gated while the UI treats it as owner-only; any workspace member can enumerate API key metadata
samples.evidence: The doc hunk under review (docs/tasks/active/20260809-workspace-settings-owner-gating-lessons.md:29-31) knowingly ships this gap: "`GET /workspaces/:id/api-keys` is only `assertMember`-gated on the backend while the UI hides the section behind `isOwner`, so that gate is cosmetic." I confirmed it: api-key.controller.ts:50 calls `assertMember` for `@Get()` whereas create (:33) and revoke (:62) call `assertOwner`, and workspace-settings.tsx:146 only issues the query when `isOwner`. Attack: any non-owner member (e.g. someone who joined via an invite link) sends `GET /workspaces/<slug>/api-keys` with their normal JWT and receives every key's id, name, prefix, scopes, expiresAt and lastUsedAt (api-key.service.ts:40-56). No secret material leaks (hashedKey/raw key are not selected) and revoke stays owner-gated, so impact is limited to metadata disclosure and reconnaissance — hence minor rather than major. The same delta that hardened `revokeInvite` documents this second scope mismatch and leaves it enforced-weaker-than-advertised.

samples.summary: `removeMember` skips every membership assertion on the self-removal branch, giving an authenticated non-member a workspace-existence oracle
samples.evidence: This delta's frontend test (`lets a non-owner member remove themselves`) and the doc hunk both newly lean on the self-removal branch, so it is worth stating what that branch actually enforces: at workspace.service.ts:92-94 the guard is skipped entirely when `requesterId === targetUserId` — neither `assertOwner` nor `assertMember` runs. Attack: any authenticated user sends `DELETE /workspaces/<slug>/members/<their own id>`; `resolveId` (line 191-203) throws `NotFoundException('Workspace not found')` for an unknown slug but the code reaches line 98 and throws `NotFoundException('Member not found')` for a real workspace they do not belong to, distinguishing existing from non-existing workspace slugs/UUIDs. No membership or data is altered (the delete on line 102 is keyed to the requester's own row), so this is enumeration/hardening rather than an access-control break. Fix would be to run `assertMember(workspaceId, requesterId)` on the self branch and return a uniform 404.

finding.summary: `revokeInvite` deletes an invite by id without scoping it to the workspace the caller owns (cross-tenant IDOR)
finding.evidence: The diff gates the revoke-invite button behind `isOwner` in the UI (workspace-settings.tsx:404) and the accompanying doc asserts "The backend authorization was already correct" (docs/tasks/active/20260809-workspace-settings-owner-gating-lessons.md:22). The enforced path does not match that claim. `WorkspaceService.revokeInvite(workspaceId, inviteId, userId)` calls `assertOwner(workspaceId, userId)` on line 138 and then executes `this.prisma.workspaceInvite.delete({ where: { id: inviteId } })` on line 139 — the `where` clause contains no `workspaceId`, so the owner check is performed against a workspace that has nothing to do with the row being deleted. Attack: user X, who is the legitimate owner of workspace A, sends `DELETE /workspaces/<A-slug>/invites/<invite-id-belonging-to-workspace-B>` (workspace.controller.ts:103-115 passes the raw path param straight through). `assertOwner` passes for A, and B's pending invite is destroyed — a cross-tenant write/denial of onboarding. Contrast `ApiKeyService.revoke(id, resolvedId)` (api-key.controller.ts:63), which does pass the workspace for scoping, showing the intended pattern. Exploitability is bounded by having to know the target invite's UUID (it is not the value in the invite link, which is `token`), so I could not complete a chain that discovers the id from outside the owning workspace — hence a missing tenant scope on a destructive operation rather than a confirmed end-to-end exploit.

verdict.reason: The claimed unscoped delete is not in the code. `WorkspaceService.revokeInvite` (workspace.service.ts:133-147) calls `assertOwner` (line 138), resolves the workspace id (line 141), and then runs `deleteMany({ where: { id: inviteId, workspaceId: resolvedId } })` (lines 142-144), throwing NotFoundException when count===0 (line 145) — the workspaceId tenant scope the finding says is absent is present, with an explanatory comment on lines 139-140 naming exactly the cross-tenant attack. Grep for `workspaceInvite\.(delete|deleteMany)` shows no `\.delete(` call anywhere in src/; the scoped deleteMany on line 142 is the only production delete path, and the sole HTTP entry point (workspace.controller.ts:103-115, JwtAuthGuard at line 22) routes into it, so the described attack (owner of A revoking B's invite) returns 404 rather than deleting. The finding also mis-quotes the doc: docs/tasks/active/20260809-workspace-settings-owner-gating-lessons.md:20-25 does not claim the backend was already correct — it documents the id-only delete as the bug and states the delete "is now a deleteMany scoped to { id, workspaceId }". Tests at workspace.service.spec.ts:394-421 assert both the scoped where-clause and the NotFoundException for another workspace's invite id.
